newsitem.title: UK: Oil prices stable as Iraq lines up more oil firms.
newsitem.headline: Oil prices stable as Iraq lines up more oil firms.

text.p: World oil prices clung to a range above the psychological $18 per barrel level on Thursday but showed little incentive to move higher in a market sitting on comfortable supply and stocks and the prospect of more Iraqi crude to come once U.N. sanctions are removed.

Iraq's oil minister was in Rome on Thursday announcing a post-sanctions line-up of foreign oil firms to develop Iraqi oil fields and raise the country's production capacity once the U.N. ban is lifted.

World benchmark Brent Blend crude oil for June delivery traded in a band between $18.05 and $18.22 a barrel on London's International Petroleum Exchange (IPE) for much of the day and was trading near the top end of the scale in the late London afternoon, up 10 cents at $18.16 a barrel by 1626 GMT.

"It appears that buyers of crude no longer feel anxiety about being able to obtain their supplies," said Michael Rothman, senior energy analyst at Merill Lynch in New York. He said the market was discounting the impact of a warmer than expected Northern hemisphere winter and the resultant rise in oil stock inventories.

"The stock situation is pretty dramatic if you compared it with just a few months ago when inventories were at 10 million barrels to 100 million barrels now, which is above the historical average for this time of the year," Rothman said.
"The data on inventories of OECD countries were very significant, suggesting that after nearly a two-year period, the oil balance has gone from tight to adequately supplied," he added.

"With OPEC not seemingly prepared to do anything to reduce their production, short of buyers not lifting oil, the markets are not subject to any upward pressure in the near to medium term unless there were to be some sort of significant geopolitical disturbance," he said.

Brokers said Organisation of the Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) producer Nigeria, where a port workers' strike earlier in the week threatened to delay some crude oil exports, was no longer a market factor. Neither was fellow OPEC producer Iraq after the United States said it would not stop Iraqi helicopter movement of Moslem pilgrims through a no-fly zone in southern Iraq.
A report from Kuwait that an Iraqi boat had fired on two Kuwaiti vessels this month also had minimum impact.

"On its own, this does not seem like a major incident, but combined with the no-fly issue, the U.N. may be forced to take action against this increased belligerence by the Iraqi regime," said brokers GNI.

"Some experts now talk of 'sanctions fatigue' among the international community, with several states keen to do business with the country. Iraqi oil is also popular with refiners," GNI added in a daily market report.

Iraqi oil minister Amir Muhammad Rasheed said in Rome that he was close to a deal on development of the Nasiriya oil field with Italy's Agip. He also said a deal was close with China for developing another oil field as part of plans to raise output capacity to six million barrels per day (bpd) compared with 2.5 million bpd currently and pre-Gulf War capacity of 3.5 million bpd.

Rasheed also said Iraq exported 750,000 barrels per day (bpd) of crude oil last week under the United Nations limited oil sales plan. He told a news conference the export figure compared with some 500,000 bpd last December when the oil-for-food plan began.

The U.N. plan allows Iraq to sell crude oil up to a value of $2 billion over six months to buy food and medicines. The return of Iraqi crude oil to the market for the first time since the August 1990 Iraqi invasion of Kuwait was partly responsible for the decline in oil prices, which in January touched $25 a barrel before falling back on the weight of supply and rising industry stocks.
OPEC is producing nearly two million bpd above its self-imposed ceiling of 25.03 million bpd, which makes provision for Iraqi exports.
